title: TA9-13425
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (herein "the claimant"), and his spouse, XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX, both citizens of Venezuela,1 seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act2 (the IRPA).

The claimant alleges that he was involved in a car incident on XXXXXX, 2007 at X o'clock in the morning whereby he hit a man who identified himself as a police officer.3 His wife, the co-claimant, was in the car with him. He called the emergency from his cell phone and the ambulance and police arrived 30 minutes later. He followed the police to the Transit Department (Instituto Nacional de Transito y Transporte Terreste - INTTT), where he provided a declaration. He spent most of the day at the INTTT and his car was retained for further investigation. Two weeks later, his lawyer got a court order to have his car released. Two weeks later, the man he had injured, a Mr. XXXXXXXXX (herein referred to as "XXX") called him, demanding $35,000,000 Boliveres pesos ($U.S.20,000) for the injuries he suffered. He went to see his lawyer, Mr. XXXXXXXX XXXXXXX, (herein referred to as "XXX") to report the extortion. He was advised that legally XXX was unable to do anything to him in court due to the impossibility of the claimant having been able to see XXX on the roadway due to the hour and the curve in the road. The claimant states in his narrative that "they have been unable to take legal action against me, even though two years have passed and all of their influences."

XXX would call the claimant at his house sometimes two or five times per day, so the claimant states that he had no choice but to go to the police to report the extortion and threats. He states in his narrative that he did so on XXXXXXXX, 2007 at the police department called Centro de Investigciones Cientificas Penales y Crimnaliisticas (CICPC). The police told him they would investigate.

On XXXXXX, 2008 the claimant and his wife were arriving home when the claimant was attacked by XXX and others who identified themselves as police officers. Due to his wife's screaming, the attackers fled in a XXXXXXXXXXXX with no license plates. The claimant sought medical attention at a clinic and reported the incident the next day to police (CICPC). After this he took his lawyer's advice and moved to another address in his city and changed his phone numbers, including his cell. However, XXX continued to call him at his new address and on his work cell frequently (three to five times per day) threatening to kill him. In XXX 2008, XXX called again, telling him that he knew where he worked and lived and that he would not escape death. He also called the claimant's wife and threatened to kill her also. They reported to the police again to make a denunciation. Once again, the police officer took their report and told them they would investigate. The claimant took his lawyer's advice and moved outside of XXXXX to the city of XXXXX, some 1 1/2 hours away.

The claimant stated in his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative and reiterated this in testimony that things were fine for seven months until on XXXXXXX, 2008, the claimant was shot at while getting into his car in his apartment's parking lot. He states that he saw XXX on the other side of the fence with another person. XXX immediately took a 9mm pistol and fired at the claimant a few times. Luckily the claimant was not harmed and he was able to recover the two bullets. He testified he reported to the police in XXXXX, however they told him to report to the police in XXXXX. He drove there, reporting to police and also gave them the bullets.4 He called his lawyer who became very concerned that the police did nothing to protect the claimant so he advised him to leave Venezuela. The claimant immediately called his friend in Canada who offered him a place to stay. They left Venezuela on XXXXXXX, 2008 and claimed protection XX months later on June 2, 2009.
I find the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Credibility, Reavailment, Delay
Having reviewed the written and oral testimony of the claimant, I find there are issues of credibility within this claim.

The claimant's narrative and oral testimony indicated that he was involved in an incident on XXXXXX, 2007 in which he struck a police officer named XXX who he believed had set up the accident in efforts to extort money from him. The claimant's explanation was that this was something quite common in Venezuela.

Upon closer review of the police reports filed by the claimant, I note two reports in which the claimant has stated that the incident with XXX occurred in 2005. The first is a report filed on XXXXXXXX, 2007,5 wherein the claimant stated that he was receiving repeated death threats by XXX who was demanding extortion from him. The second question posed of the claimant was, "Do you know Mr. XXXXXXXXXXXX? ANSWER: "Yes, he is a police officer assigned to Municipal Police of XXXX, what happened is that on XXXXXX, 2005, I hit Mr. XXXX XXXXXXXX with my motor vehicle and he was injured in that accident. The third question was, "did you receive threats after the accident? ANSWER: Yes, the same day of the accident, I transported XXXXXXXXXXXX to a clinic, and at that place came several Municipal Police of XXX, who threatened me several times. The fourth question was, "Did you announce the threats mentioned in the previous answer? ANSWER: I NOTIFIED TO THE Fiscal Third of XXXX State, who was looking into the accident, but I don't know what steps they are taking in this regard. On XXXXX, 2008,6 the claimant reported he was assaulted by Mr. XXXXXXXXXXXX in front of his wife in the parking lot of his home on the evening of XXXXXX, 2008 at 9:30 pm. The second question posed to the claimant when interviewed by an officer was, "Do you know aggressors?" The claimant's answer was, "Yes, one of them is XXXXXXXXX, he is a police officer of the Municipal Police of XXXX, and in 2005 I hit him with my car and since then he is constantly threaten me." Clearly the dates in these two reports filed in XXXXXX 2007 and XXXXX 2008 refer to the initial incident with XXX as happening in 2005. Obviously this date is two years previous to the date the claimant indicated on his PIF narrative and in testimony. This inconsistency was not noticed at the hearing and therefore the claimant was not asked to explain the discrepancy. As a result, I am simply at this time noting the inconsistency between official police reports and the claimant's PIF and testimony. I note as well that the claimant's lawyer, XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, has provided a statement which states that he arrived at the scene of the accident involving XXX which he indicates was on XXXXXXX, 2007. I am unable to assign much weight to this statement as it is not notarized, has no date on it nor do I find his name or signature on any of the police reports or any witness statements made by him to police regarding the XXXXX 2007 incident which he states he was present at the scene two hours after it happened.

At the hearing, however, questions were put to the claimant regarding his travel outside of Venezuela. For example the claimant departed Venezuela for Panama on XXXXXXXX, 2007, returning from that visit on XXXXXXXX, 2007. He then left for a business trip to Miami on XXXXXX, 2007 and returned the same day. According to his evidence, the initial encounter and incident with XXX happened the following day on XXXXXX, 2007. The claimant then left for another visit to Panama on XXXXXXXX, 2007, returning on XXXXXXXX, 2007.7 I note it was after this XXXXXX, 2007 incident in which he stated in his narrative and reiterated in his testimony was the precipitating incident causing him problems. The claimant was asked why he returned to Venezuela if he was being extorted and threatened by XXX. The claimant responded, "I went there for work and up to that point in time, there had been no attempts to kill me." I note however the claimant's PIF indicated that this trip was that of a visitor.

Notwithstanding the inconsistency regarding the purpose of that visit to Panama, I find that the claimant's travel to and re-availment to Venezuela on XXXXXXX, 2007 is inconsistent with his alleged fear of persecution or a threat to his life at the hands of XXX. Similarly, I find the claimant's return from a 10-day business trip to Miami, from XXXXXX to XXXXXX 2008, is indicative of a lack of subjective fear given his having been beaten by XXX on XXXXXX, 2008, as reported to police the following day, the repeated phone threats at his workplace, at home and on his and his wife's cell phones, including the XXXX, 2008 phone call which the claimant states in paragraph 13 of his narrative, threatened to kill both he and his wife. I note that the claimant states in the police report file to this last call, on XXXX, 2008,8 that his wife has not been physically attacked but "threatened her by phone constantly and she is suffering a nervous breakdown as consequences of the harassment." It was this call, which, upon advice of his lawyer, forced them to move to XXXX in XXX 2008. Given these reports and statements made within them by the claimant, I am unable to assign any weight to the claimant's explanation when asked the reasons for returning to Venezuela on XXXXXX, 2008 given that he had, according to statements made in his narrative, been threatened with death by XXX, such that it caused him to move to XXXX and these three denunciations made to police. Additionally, I find it not credible that the claimant would leave his wife in XXXX to travel to the United States if he believed XXX's threat that he knew where the claimant's lived and worked. However, given the move to XXXX, the claimant's testimony that he returned to XXXX approximately 15 times such as to pick up checks when payment had been made to his employer, XXXX (who he began working for in XXXX 2008) and his statement that "everything was fine" until XXXXXX, 2008 when XXX shot at him, I conclude that he did not possess a subjective fear until that incident on XXXXXX, 2008.

The claimant's testimony and evidence indicates that he and his wife moved to XXXX in XXX 2008 and also changed their jobs.9 However, the claimant's employment history shows that the claimant took on a job as XXXXXXXXXX of a company in XXXX from XXXX 2008 to XXXXX, 2008, which he indicated was a business owned by a relative and I note previous to the XXXXX phone calls from XXX which threatened to kill him and his wife. The claimant was asked about this other job and why he no longer worked there after XXXX, 2008. He testified that it did not provide sufficient income. He then returned to XXXXXXXXXXXXX for a company called XXXXXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXX, 2008. His last date of work with this company was XXXXXXX, 2008, the day before his departure, however he explained that he did not notify the company until after he arrived in Canada.

I find, had the claimant possessed a well-founded fear of persecution, he would have not returned to Venezuela after his trips abroad, paerticularly to the U.S. in XXXXX 2008 or to Panama before that. Regardless of whether the initial icident with XXX happened in 2005 or 2007, I find that the claimant's delay in departing Venezuela until XXXXXX 2008 impugns his credibility. As stated earlier, I have assigned little weight to his explanation regarding why he would return to Venezuela given the repeated death threats and attempts to extort money from him. Delay has been recognized by the Federal Court as an important factor in assessing a claimant's credibility and their subjective fear. It is reasonable to assume that persons with a well-founded fear of persecution will attempt to flee and apply for refugee protection without unreasonable delay.10 While delay in making a refugee claim is not in itself usually decisive, it is a relevant factor to be considered when assessing the overall viability of the claim.11

In conclusion, on a balance of evidence provided regarding the claimant's particular circumstances, including the claimant's repeated returns to XXXX, the city in which he lived previous to XXXX, and this is the city where the incident with XXXX took place, the city where he received numerous threatening calls to his workplace, home and cellular and the city he left because of these threats, I find that the claimant did not possess a subjective fear particularly given his testimony that he had no further contact with XXX between XXXX 2008 and the shooting incident of XXXXXX, 2008. This lack of fear is corroborated by the claimant's own actions of returning from a trip abroad as late as XXXXXX 2008.

Further, I am unable to find plausible that the police in XXXX would not take a report or investigate the XXXXXX, 2008 incident regarding the attempted murder of the claimant by XXX. The claimant's testimony was that he was told by the police in XXXX that he had to report this incident to the police in XXXX because reports had been filed with them previously. I find that this does not make any sense because it would provide evidence that XXX had traveled to XXXX for the purpose of an attempted murder which would obviously provide evidence from a third party (notably part of the state security apparatus) to support the claimant's previous denunciations and investigations that were apparently being conducted by the CICPC. Notwithstanding, the XXXXXX, 2008 police report has been filed into evidence and more about this shall be discussed below under state protection.

In addition, given the claimant's visits for work or otherwise to Panama, Miami or Los Angeles, I find that his not having sought asylum in the United States or Panama undermines the credibility of his alleged fear of persecution.

The claimant delayed making his claim for protection for six months after arriving in Canada. His explanation was that he believed that he had to support his claim with corroborative evidence. I am unable to assign any weight to this explanation given the claimant's testimony that he had a friend living in Canada who it would appear from CIC notes, was the same friend who had invited him to Canada in 2005, which happens to have been the year that police reports indicate that the initial encounter with XXX occurred.

I note that the claimant and his wife were denied in their applications for Canadian visas in 2005. It appears that after an interview with an Embassy official, the denial was due to an employment letter not appearing to be an original and, after the interview, the officer's finding was that they did not appear bonafide visitors. Subsequent notes on the CIC file indicate that the claimants reapplied and were granted Canadian visas on the basis that they were leaving a child in Venezuela, the presentation of many documents showing employment with good incomes and that the stated purpose of the visa was for a side-trip to Canada from New York City, United States. The XXXXXX, 2005 denial for Canadian visas in 200512 was explored at the hearing, however, given the 2005 date in the reports had not been put to the claimant, I am unable but to note that it is coincidental that the claimants' first attempt to leave Venezuela for whatever purpose was soon after the date as it stated by the claimant in statements made by him in the XXXXXX 2007 and XXXXXX 2008 reports, which was XXXXXX, 2005.

Irrespective of my credibility concerns due to inconsistencies in which the initial incident with XXX occurred whether it was in 2005 or 2007, or my finding that the claimant's repeated reavailment to Venezuela in 2007 and 2008 indicates a lack of subjective fear, or my concern that the claimants did not make their claims for protection until after being in Canada for six months, the determinative issue, even were I not to have credibility concerns, is that of state protection.

Referring to my earlier discussion of credibility, I have found that the claimant re-availed to Venezuela numerous times prior to 2008, clearly indicating that he possessed no subjective fear. After the incident of XXXXXX, 2008 and his having reported the alleged shooting by XXX to police on that same date, the claimants delayed leaving the country for over two weeks after having been issued Canadian visas, even though they had valid U.S. visas which were issued in XXXX 2007. I again determine that this is inconsistent with a subjective fear as it is unreasonable for them not to have left at the very first opportunity. In addition to my finding that they did not possess a well-founded fear of persecution, I find that the circumstances of the claimant and his fear of a rogue police officer, who was attempting to extort, threaten and kill the claimant, is a fear of criminality.

The claimants have stated to immigration officials that they fear XXX but also the government because they are against the Chavez government. I am unable to assign any weight to their stating that they did not receive protection from the government because of their anti-Chavez government beliefs. However, in the circumstances of this case, counsel has conceded that the circumstances of these claimants fall under section 97 and that the determinative issue is that of state protection. Persons in Need of Protection, s. 97, Immigration and Refugee Protection Act State Protection

The next issue in this case is whether the principal claimant would, on a balance of probabilities,13 be subjected to a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if he were to return to Venezuela.

In assessing the issue of state protection, I am guided by a number of cases. There is a presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown.14 A claimant, who alleges that state protection is not available, must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate.15 A claimant can rebut the presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might reasonably be forthcoming.16

No government can be expected to guarantee perfect protection of all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim. This is particularly true when a state is in effective control of its territory and has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious attempts to protect its citizens.17

The burden of proving an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy that exists in the state.18 The documentary evidence before the Board indicates Venezuela is a functioning democracy.19 It has functioning political and judicial systems in place, and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.20

Venezuela is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces, both military and police, in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country. Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.21 The Venezuelan security forces are hierarchical and allow a person to complain to a higher authority if dissatisfied with the services provided. The National Guard, a branch of the military that maintains order, is complemented by state and local police services, as well as city forces in the major centers such as XXXX.22

Counsel has submitted that the claimants sought protection on four occasions and that the police did not arrest XXX even though they said they would investigate. I agree with counsel that the documentary evidence currently before the Board shows that the police in Venezuela continue to struggle with issues of corruption and criminality. However, efforts to change are also shown with the documents before the Board. In a recent report,23 Chavez created a new National Police Force, a force which pays "three times the current average police salary" and which the Justice Minister described as "...a decent body, irreproachable and ethical for which we must ensure proper conduct by officials."

Further, the Ministry of the Interior appears to be dealing with the issues of police misconduct in Venezuela and currently 1,800 of 9,000 police officers are under investigation by the Ministry.24 The recent Department of State Report for 2010 indicated that impunity remains a problem however police officers, who have committed abuses, are being prosecuted. This report states that in 2010 there were over 9,610 complaints made against police officers and even evidence provided on behalf of the claimants25 indicates police officers had been arrested. While this evidence implies that those 6 officers did not have links to higher authorities to assist them such as higher government officials, the claimant in the circumstances of his situation has not provided any evidence to suggest that XXX was connected to any higher leveled official. When asked about this, he responded that all police work for the government and they cover each other's back.

In the circumstances of this claim, it is clear that the claimant was not reluctant to file denunciations with the police even though he believes that they cover each other's back. He did so several times; the last time the same month as he departed Venezuela for the final time. While police reports show that XXX was named by the claimant as the perpetrator of threats, beatings and the attempt against his life in XXXXXX 2008, when questioned about what the police told him, the claimant replied that the police indicated that there was little to investigate if there was no proof of who made the calls or there were no witnesses to attacks made upon him. Even so, I find that, if the claimants were dissatisfied with the attention or lack service provided by police, they had other avenues to pursue such as higher levels of police authorities. When asked about this, the claimant responded that he had a lawyer who reported to the police and the Attorney General, and his lawyer was of the opinion that the police were not doing anything and told him to flee. While I can find it unreasonable that the claimant returned to the same police authorities in XXXX if he indeed believed they were not doing anything, I find that, under the circumstances, he could have complained to the Ministry of the Interior as documentation indicates they are actively investigating police misconduct in that country.

The Federal Court has ruled that the fact that the persecutor was a police officer does not mean that the state itself is the agent of persecution, or that state protection is not available. It also does not relieve the claimant from seeking available redress before seeking protection from another state.26 Further, the behavior of some police officers does not obviate the need to seek the protection from the authorities since that is not sufficient proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens.27

I find that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that there is inadequate state protection in Venezuela, nor has he taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to pursue the available state protection.28 I find the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and the claim fails under s. 97 of the IRPA.
The claimant's wife relies on the claimant's claim and thus her claim fails as well.

Having given due consideration to all of the evidence before it, the relevant provisions of the IRPA, and to the jurisprudence upon which the Board relies, I find the claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. Accordingly, these claims for refugee protection are rejected.
